categories.title: Glass Tower Modern
categories.description: The Glass Tower Modern archetype represents the dominant form of contemporary urban office development: a full-curtain-wall tower rising from a distinguished podium base, delivering large floor-plate commercial office space to dense downtown cores. The typology ranges from rectilinear corporate slabs clad in reflective blue or dark tinted glass, to parametric sculpted towers with undulating balcony spandrels and integrated sky gardens. Ground-floor lobbies are expressed as transparent, double-height volumes with premium stone or structural glass entries that activate the street edge. Facades emphasize vertical continuity, with aluminum mullion grids, reflective glazing, and occasional setback crowns or spire elements marking the skyline. These towers anchor financial districts and mixed-use corridors, projecting corporate prestige while offering flexible, open-plan floorplates across a wide range of scales.

styleProfile.facadeRhythm: continuous vertical grid of floor-to-ceiling glazing panels punctuated by horizontal spandrels or projecting balcony bands
styleProfile.roofForm: flat or chamfered crown with spire or antenna element; some variants feature rooftop terrace gardens or tapered sculpted peaks
styleProfile.frontageType: double-height glazed lobby set within stone podium, with canopy overhang and street-level plaza or landscaped apron
styleProfile.windowStyle: full-height curtain-wall units, floor-to-ceiling, in blue reflective, clear, or dark tinted glass with aluminum framing
styleProfile.massing: slender rectilinear or gently tapered tower shaft above a wider podium base; some variants adopt a curvilinear or sculpted profile
styleProfile.heightTendency: mid-rise to high-rise, 8 to 30 storeys depending on variant and urban density context
styleProfile.streetRelationship: podium base engages sidewalk with lobby canopy, plaza trees, and retail-ready transparency; tower setback from street line above base
styleProfile.renderingMood: crisp daylight or golden-hour urban render with sky reflections in glazing, surrounding context buildings, and street-level trees
styleProfile.articulation: vertical mullion lines dominate shaft; podium distinguished by stone cladding and cantilevered canopy; crown differentiated by chamfer, taper, or planted terrace
styleProfile.publicRealm: landscaped plaza or wide sidewalk apron with mature street trees, entry canopy, and active glazed ground floor

prompt.subject: A contemporary glass-curtain-wall office tower rising from a polished stone podium base in a dense urban downtown setting.
details: Full-height reflective glazing across tower shaft with aluminum mullion grid and visible floor spandrels
Ground-floor lobby expressed as double-height transparent volume within a marble or granite podium with projecting canopy
Tower crown differentiated by chamfered setback, sculptural taper, or rooftop terrace planting
Surrounding context of mid-rise brick and concrete buildings framing the tower at street level
Street-level trees, wide sidewalk, and warm interior lobby glow visible through ground-floor glazing
Sky reflections and cloud movement captured in the curtain-wall surface, conveying corporate prestige and urban scale

archetypes.title: New York Art Deco Tower
archetypes.description: 1920s-1930s Art Deco office tower shaped by the 1916 Zoning Resolution's setback requirements. Sculptural stepped massing rises from a broad base through wedding-cake setbacks to an ornamental crown or spire. Facades clad in limestone and polychrome terra cotta with geometric zigzag, chevron, and sunburst motifs. Verticality emphasized by uninterrupted piers between spandrel panels. Elaborate lobby interiors with marble, bronze, and murals. Exemplified by the Chrysler Building, Empire State Building, and One Wall Street.

archetypes.title: New York Pre-War Apartment
archetypes.description: Grand pre-war apartment building from 1900-1940, the golden age of luxury Manhattan residential architecture. 6-15 floors in brick with limestone trim, featuring elaborate cornices, ornamental terra cotta, decorative water towers, and generous floor plans with formal rooms. Landmark examples include the San Remo, the Beresford, and the Eldorado.

archetypes.title: New York Walk-Up Tenement
archetypes.description: New York walk-up tenement building from the 1860s-1920s, the dominant housing type of immigrant New York. 5-6 storey narrow brick buildings built under Old Law (1879) or New Law (1901) tenement regulations. Dumbbell-plan air shafts, ornate pressed-metal or stone cornices, cast-iron fire escapes, and elaborate Italianate or Queen Anne facade ornament belie the cramped interiors. The fire escape has become an iconic symbol of New York streetscape character.

archetypes.title: Hydrostone Neighbourhood House
archetypes.description: Distinctive Hydrostone neighbourhood house from the 1918-1920 reconstruction of Halifax's North End after the devastating 1917 Halifax Explosion. archetypes.title: Modernisme Casa
archetypes.description: Catalan Modernisme (Art Nouveau) residential building from 1888-1911, the golden age of Barcelona's cultural and architectural renaissance. 3-5 storey residential buildings featuring organic curvilinear forms, ornate wrought-iron balconies, colorful ceramic tile (trencadis) cladding, carved stone facades with naturalistic motifs, and stained glass. archetypes.title: Vancouver Laneway House
archetypes.description: Detached accessory dwelling unit built at the rear of single-family lots along Vancouver's back lanes, legalized by the city's 2009 zoning bylaw. Over 7,000 have been built since 2009, representing a key form of 'gentle densification' and missing-middle housing. Designs range from contemporary flat-roof boxes to gabled forms harmonizing with the main house character.

archetypes.title: Vancouver Special
archetypes.description: The only house style unique to Greater Vancouver, built by the thousands between 1965 and 1985. A front-gabled two-storey box built on grade with a very shallow-pitched roof, designed to maximize square footage on narrow 33-foot lots by exploiting a zoning loophole that excluded basements from floor area calculations. Characterized by a distinctive shallow upper balcony with iron or aluminum railings, decorative brick on the ground-floor front facade with stucco above, and a front door set to one side for easy up-down duplex conversion. The city changed its building code in 1985 to prevent further construction of this style.

archetypes.title: Vancouverism Tower-Podium
archetypes.description: The signature building typology of 'Vancouverism' — a slender residential point tower rising from a low-rise townhouse or retail podium that defines the street edge. Developed from the 1990s onward, this urban design model combines New York brownstone-inspired podiums with Hong Kong-inspired slim towers to preserve views, maximize density, and maintain street-level vibrancy. Podiums typically 3-6 storeys with townhouse units, retail, and amenity space, while towers above are slender enough (typically under 20m floor plate width) to allow light and views between buildings.

archetypes.title: Airport Terminal Building
archetypes.description: Airport terminal buildings are large-span civic infrastructure typologies that combine passenger processing, retail concessions, and gate access under dramatic roof structures. Their architectural character is defined by the tension between engineering spectacle — expressed trusses, vaulted canopies, cable-stayed masts — and the efficient movement of thousands of people per hour. Facades tend toward transparency at the landside frontage, with glazed curtain walls or arched fenestration inviting natural light into departure halls. Scale ranges from compact regional terminals to multi-gate complexes, each variant distinguished by structural language, era, and material philosophy. The building type consistently prioritizes civic legibility: a recognizable silhouette, generous canopy overhangs at drop-off, and a strong street presence that signals arrival.

archetypes.title: Annex Mansion
archetypes.description: The Annex Mansion is a grand late-Victorian detached residence characteristic of Toronto's Annex neighbourhood, built predominantly between the 1880s and 1910s for upper-middle-class and professional families. These large, freestanding homes are distinguished by their Richardsonian Romanesque or Queen Anne massing, featuring corner turrets, steeply pitched multi-gabled roofs, elaborate carved stone or brick ornamentation, and generous wrap-around verandahs. Facades typically combine rusticated sandstone or rock-faced granite with polychrome brick, creating richly textured streetscapes that sit close to the sidewalk behind low iron fencing. The program historically centred on a single grand household but many examples have since been converted to multi-unit dwellings or professional offices while retaining their architectural character. As landmark presences on residential streets, Annex Mansions anchor neighbourhood identity and set a high bar for heritage-sensitive infill and renovation.

archetypes.title: Aquatic Natatorium Complex
archetypes.description: The aquatic natatorium complex is a large-span civic building type purpose-built to enclose Olympic or competition-grade swimming pools, leisure pools, and hydrotherapy facilities under a single expansive roof structure. The typology demands exceptional interior volume — typically 10–18 m clear height over pool halls — achieved through arched, vaulted, or cable-tensioned structural systems that also provide natural daylighting. Architecturally, natatoriums span a wide range of expression, from parametric sculptural shells in polycarbonate and tensioned steel to heritage Beaux-Arts bath-houses with cast-iron and glass barrel vaults, biophilic mass-timber arches with living roofs, and functional community recreation centres in profiled metal cladding. The building type sits at the intersection of civic infrastructure and public wellness, often serving as a landmark sports destination or neighbourhood health hub. Facades are characterised by large expanses of glazing to animate pool interiors and mediate condensation and humidity loads.

archetypes.title: Bay and Gable House
archetypes.description: The Bay and Gable House is a quintessential Victorian-era urban residential typology found predominantly in late-19th-century Canadian and American cities, characterized by a projecting front bay window rising one or two storeys and crowned by a decorative gabled dormer. The form combines Italianate massing with Gothic Revival ornamental detailing — scroll-cut bargeboards, finials, polychrome brick banding, and arched window surrounds — producing a richly articulated street presence on a compact semi-detached or detached lot. Facades typically employ load-bearing brick construction in buff, red, or cream tones, with contrasting brick voussoirs, stone sills, and painted wood trim providing rhythmic colour contrast. The typology sits flush or near-flush to the sidewalk, contributing to continuous streetwall definition in older inner-city neighbourhoods. As a duplex form it often accommodates two stacked residential units behind an architecturally unified Victorian frontage.

archetypes.title: Biophilic Modern Healthcare
archetypes.description: Biophilic Modern Healthcare facilities integrate nature-forward design principles with clinical and wellness programming, prioritising patient wellbeing through direct exposure to greenery, natural light, and organic materials. These buildings weave living walls, rooftop gardens, and timber structural systems into their architectural language, creating environments that measurably reduce stress and accelerate recovery. The typology spans from compact urban clinics and community health centres to mid-rise specialist hospitals and wellness campuses, each grounded in a commitment to low-carbon construction and renewable energy integration. Facades are treated as ecological surfaces — solar panels, vertical gardens, timber louvres, and carved stone work in concert to blur the boundary between built form and landscape. The result is an institutional building type that reads as simultaneously calming and technologically progressive.

archetypes.title: Boutique Hotel
archetypes.description: The boutique hotel typology encompasses intimate, design-forward lodging properties that prioritize distinct architectural identity over standardized hospitality formats. Typically occupying 20–80 rooms across 3–20 storeys, these buildings express strong curatorial intent through materials, massing, and street presence. Programs combine guest rooms with curated food-and-beverage, rooftop amenities, and activated ground-floor lobbies that engage the public realm. Architectural character ranges from adaptive reuse of historic fabric to purpose-built contemporary statements, unified by an emphasis on experiential arrival sequences and high-craft detailing. The typology thrives across urban neighborhoods, resort towns, and waterfront districts, anchoring its surroundings with a sense of place-specificity.

archetypes.title: Brick Rowhouse Terrace
archetypes.description: The brick rowhouse terrace is a quintessential urban residential typology characterized by attached or semi-detached dwellings sharing party walls along a continuous street frontage. Rooted in Victorian and Edwardian building traditions, these terraces combine load-bearing red or dark-brown brick construction with decorative stone dressings, ornamental gabled rooflines, and rhythmically repeating window bays. The typology spans from highly ornamented Gothic Revival and Queen Anne terraces to plainer Edwardian semi-detached pairs and contemporary infill rowhouses with rooftop additions. Street presence is defined by low iron railings or hedged front gardens that maintain a clear threshold between public pavement and private entry. The archetype is well suited to inner-suburban and urban residential streets, delivering medium-density housing with strong neighbourhood character and heritage appeal.

archetypes.title: Calgary 15 Connected Tower
archetypes.description: The Calgary 15 Connected Tower is a mid-rise to high-rise office typology defined by its integration with Calgary's iconic +15 elevated pedestrian skywalk network, which links buildings at the second-floor level across downtown. These structures typically occupy full urban blocks or prominent corner sites, presenting assertive street-level podiums that connect directly to the enclosed walkway bridges. The archetype encompasses a spectrum from 1970s–80s brutalist-inflected concrete office slabs to contemporary curtain-wall towers with mixed-use podiums, all sharing the defining covered bridge connector as a civic and commercial amenity. Program typically includes ground-floor retail or lobby, office floors above, and in newer iterations, residential or hospitality uses in upper tower segments. The connected-tower typology is emblematic of Calgary's downtown urban form and cold-climate design culture.

archetypes.title: Campus Dining Hall Food Court
archetypes.description: Campus dining halls and food courts serve as the social heart of university campuses, combining high-volume food service with flexible gathering space for students, faculty, and staff. These mid-rise civic buildings typically occupy prominent corner or quad-facing sites, employing a hybrid program of servery kitchen, multi-station food court, and open dining floors with generous daylighting. Architecturally, they balance institutional durability — load-bearing brick, concrete structure — with inviting transparency through large curtain-wall glazing that animates the street edge and signals public life within. Upper-level seating with terrace or mezzanine access, visible from the exterior, reinforces the communal character. Contemporary campus dining facilities often integrate sustainable features such as green roofs, warm wood cladding, and bicycle infrastructure to reflect campus sustainability goals.

archetypes.title: Campus Lecture Hall Complex
archetypes.description: The campus lecture hall complex is a purpose-built institutional education facility housing large-capacity tiered auditoria, seminar rooms, and student gathering spaces. These buildings serve as intellectual and social anchors on university campuses, ranging from intimate mass-timber pavilions to monumental brutalist blocks and expressive parametric structures. Architecturally they are distinguished by their bold civic presence, generous entrance lobbies, and the architectural challenge of expressing large-volume interior spaces — raked seating floors, acoustic enclosures, and service cores — on the exterior. The typology spans mid-century concrete monumentalism, contemporary biophilic timber construction, sculptural parametric forms, and organic vernacular-inspired designs, each reflecting different eras and institutional cultures of higher education.

archetypes.title: Campus Parking Structure
archetypes.description: Campus parking structures are multi-storey vehicle storage facilities designed to integrate with educational campuses and urban institutional contexts. These structures balance functional efficiency — long-span open decks, ramped circulation, and high-throughput entry/exit lanes — with contextual architectural expression that responds to adjacent campus buildings. Facades are typically screened or articulated to mask the utilitarian interior while presenting a civic face to the street, using materials such as brick, precast concrete panels, and metal louver screens. Corner stair towers, glazed elevator lobbies, and ground-floor retail or pedestrian-active frontages are common devices for urban compatibility. Floor-to-floor heights are taller than typical office construction to accommodate vehicle clearance, resulting in compact but visually substantial massing at 4–6 storeys.

archetypes.title: Campus Recreation Athletics Centre

Street-level frontages prioritize pedestrian access with canopied entries, bike parking, and landscaped setbacks that animate the campus edge.

archetypes.title: Central Utilities Plant Energy Centre
archetypes.description: A central utilities plant or energy centre is a purpose-built urban infrastructure building housing mechanical and electrical plant — boilers, chillers, cooling towers, heat exchangers, and switchgear — that serves a district, campus, or dense mixed-use precinct. Architecturally, these buildings must reconcile heavy industrial servicing requirements (large ductwork penetrations, rooftop mechanical equipment, ventilation louvers) with urban-context sensitivity, resulting in facades that blend exposed structural honesty with masonry or cladding treatments. The typology ranges from compact 2–3 storey infill plant rooms set flush to the street grid, to taller 4–5 storey anchor buildings with expressed mechanical penthouses and glazed curtain-wall faces that reveal the machinery within. Common to all variants is the presence of visible infrastructure elements — exhaust stacks, cooling tower banks, large louver arrays, and surface-mounted pipework — treated as architectural features rather than afterthoughts.

archetypes.title: Chateauesque Grand Railway Hotel
archetypes.description: The Chateauesque Grand Railway Hotel is a monumental late-Victorian hospitality typology conceived at the height of transcontinental railway expansion, when competing rail companies commissioned castle-like flagship hotels to anchor urban termini and mountain resort towns. Drawing on French Renaissance château forms filtered through Scottish baronial and Gothic Revival influences, these buildings are characterized by asymmetric massing, conical tourelles, steeply pitched slate roofs, and lavish stone carving that projected civic grandeur and national ambition. Programs typically encompass grand ballrooms, formal dining rooms, and several hundred guest rooms arranged along double-loaded corridors within a U- or L-shaped perimeter block. The street presence is deliberately theatrical — crenellated parapets, heraldic stone reliefs, and arched porte-cochères signal arrival and ceremony to guests approaching from street level. Across its four historical variants the typology ranges from raw-granite Scottish-baronial towers to cream Beaux-Arts limestone blocks, High Victorian Gothic limestone halls, and Alpine chalet-influenced resort wings.

archetypes.title: Collegiate Gothic
archetypes.description: Collegiate Gothic is a historicist architectural tradition rooted in the medieval universities of Oxford and Cambridge, adapted across Britain and North America for academic, administrative, and ceremonial institutional buildings. The typology is defined by load-bearing stone or brick masonry, pointed Gothic arches, elaborate tracery windows, crenellated parapets, and vertical towers that signal institutional permanence and scholarly authority. Buildings are typically arranged around quadrangles or set as freestanding civic monuments along urban streets, with richly articulated facades that combine heraldic stonework, oriel windows, and decorative finials. The program encompasses lecture halls, libraries, collegiate common rooms, and administrative suites, often within a single monumental block. Rendered in warm limestone, red brick, or polychrome masonry, the aesthetic conveys learned tradition, civic gravitas, and aspirational heritage.

archetypes.title: Condo Podium Tower
archetypes.description: The condo podium tower is a mixed-use residential high-rise typology defined by a distinct two-part massing: a street-activating podium base of 2–4 storeys housing retail or amenity programs, topped by a slender residential tower. This form mediates between the pedestrian scale of the street and the vertical ambition of urban density, making it a cornerstone of contemporary North American urban infill. Facades range from contextual red-brick podiums with glass curtain-wall towers to parametric curved forms and heritage retrofit bases, reflecting a broad stylistic spectrum. Balconies, expressed floor plates, and generous glazing are consistent tower characteristics regardless of variant. The typology typically delivers 80–300+ units per building, serving mid- to high-density residential growth in established urban neighbourhoods.

archetypes.title: Contemporary Midrise
archetypes.description: Contemporary midrise residential buildings represent the dominant infill typology in urban neighborhoods undergoing densification, typically occupying narrow lots between 15–30 m wide and rising 5–9 storeys above street level. These buildings balance unit efficiency with architectural ambition, featuring articulated facades, integrated balconies, and high glazing ratios that animate the street edge. Programs typically include ground-floor residential lobbies or retail, stacked market-rate or mixed-income apartments, and rooftop amenity space. The typology spans a wide stylistic range — from warm mass-timber and biophilic curtain-wall expressions to crisp European white-render volumes and contextual brick compositions — allowing it to fit within both heritage streetscapes and emerging contemporary corridors. Quality of facade articulation, material warmth, and planting integration increasingly define the premium tier of this building type.

archetypes.title: Convention Exhibition Center
archetypes.description: Convention and exhibition centers are large-span civic structures designed to host trade shows, conferences, public events, and cultural gatherings at an urban or regional scale. They typically feature column-free exhibition halls, flexible pre-function lobbies, and prominent civic frontages that signal public welcome. Architecturally the typology ranges from dramatic tensile and glass high-tech enclosures to biophilic mass-timber pavilions, parametric blob-form facades, and adaptive reuse of industrial heritage buildings. Their large footprints demand strong street-level engagement through canopies, glazed lobbies, and generous plazas that mediate between the megastructure and the pedestrian realm. The building form is driven by interior clear-span requirements, resulting in bold roof expressions — tensile membranes, sawtooth skylights, green roofs, or undulating composite panels — that become civic landmarks.

archetypes.title: Corner Dépanneur
archetypes.description: The corner dépanneur is a quintessentially Québécois urban typology — a small-format convenience store occupying a chamfered or angled street corner lot, typically embedded within a residential neighbourhood fabric. Ranging from single-storey post-war vernacular to two-storey mixed-use blocks with a dwelling above the shop, these buildings anchor pedestrian life at intersections and serve as informal community landmarks. Architecturally modest and highly legible, they are defined by large display windows, hand-painted or mounted signage advertising lotto, bière froide, and cigarettes, and façades that accumulate decades of commercial ephemera. The typology spans eras from weathered mid-century stucco-over-brick to Art Deco corner blocks to tidy post-war red-brick mixed-use, and increasingly to renovated contemporary infill retaining the brick shell while updating the ground-floor retail expression.

archetypes.title: Corporate Office Campus Headquarters
archetypes.description: The Corporate Office Campus Headquarters archetype encompasses purpose-built office environments designed to project institutional authority, brand identity, and organizational scale. These buildings range from sleek contemporary curtain-wall rotundas to neoclassical civic-scaled headquarters, biophilic mass-timber campuses, and adaptive industrial loft conversions. Program typically includes executive suites, collaborative workspaces, ground-floor reception lobbies, and landscaped public forecourts. Architectural character shifts dramatically across the typology spectrum — from the sculptural and formal to the raw and industrial — reflecting the diverse aesthetic philosophies of modern corporate culture. Each variant anchors a distinct urban or campus context, from downtown street corners to repurposed warehouse districts.

archetypes.title: Cruise Ferry Terminal
archetypes.description: Cruise and ferry terminals are large-span waterfront civic buildings that serve as gateways between land and sea, combining ticketing, customs, passenger processing, and retail into a single monumental hall. The typology ranges from expressive contemporary structures with sculpted rooflines to beaux-arts civic monuments inherited from the golden age of ocean travel, and from sustainable mass-timber pavilions to utilitarian steel-clad operational sheds. Their principal architectural challenge is spanning vast interior volumes to accommodate passenger flows while creating a legible public face toward the city and an operational berth interface toward the water. Facades are typically horizontal and low-to-mid-rise, with emphasis on roof expression rather than vertical height. The building acts simultaneously as an urban landmark, a logistical machine, and a threshold experience announcing arrival or departure.

archetypes.title: E Commerce Fulfillment Center
archetypes.description: E-commerce fulfillment centers are large-footprint, logistics-intensive industrial buildings designed to receive, sort, store, and dispatch consumer goods at high velocity. The typology spans from heritage brick warehouses retrofitted with modern operations to purpose-built mega-sheds with automated racking systems, and increasingly encompasses sustainable formats featuring mass-timber structure, living roofs, and solar arrays. Architecturally, the program demands wide column-free floor plates, abundant dock-door bays along one or more facades, and ancillary office or mezzanine volumes that read as distinct elements against the main shed. The building's scale and repetitive dock-door rhythm define its street character, while sustainability mandates are pushing roofscape treatments — solar PV, sedum, and green corridors — into prominent design features.

styleProfile.heightTendency: low-rise to mid-rise (2–5 storeys equivalent height), with tall clear internal floor-to-ceiling heights
styleProfile.streetRelationship: set back behind a generous truck apron and service yard; office entry faces public street while dock doors face service road

archetypes.title: Early 20th Century Megastructure
archetypes.description: Early 20th century industrial megastructures represent the monumental factory and rail-infrastructure buildings of the 1900–1940 period, characterized by vast single-storey or low-rise volumes designed to shelter large-span manufacturing, assembly, or logistics operations. These buildings pioneered the combination of load-bearing brick perimeter walls with exposed steel or timber truss roof systems, clerestory and sawtooth glazing for daylighting deep floor plates, and heavy concrete base courses capable of receiving rail spurs and heavy freight. Their architectural character oscillates between raw utilitarian pragmatism and a restrained industrial classicism, with regularly spaced pilasters, corbelled brick cornices, and rhythmic multi-pane steel-sash windows conferring a monumental dignity to production at scale. Today these structures are prized for adaptive reuse as creative offices, event halls, and cultural venues, their exposed structural skeletons and patinated materiality conveying an authenticity that contemporary construction cannot replicate.

archetypes.title: Edwardian Foursquare
archetypes.description: The Edwardian Foursquare is a quintessentially North American residential typology from the 1900s–1915 era, characterized by its boxy, nearly cubic two-storey massing, hipped or pyramidal roof, and full-width front porch. The plan is organized around a central stair with four rooms per floor — the origin of the 'foursquare' name — yielding efficient, symmetrical facades with regularly spaced double-hung windows. Architectural character ranges from austere red-brick vernacular to stucco-and-half-timber Arts-and-Crafts hybrids, natural stone Craftsman variants, and adaptive-reuse conversions with contemporary additions. The type dominates mature urban residential neighbourhoods across Canada and the American Midwest, typically set on modest lots with shallow front yards and prominent porch stoops. Its enduring appeal lies in the combination of generous interior volume, straightforward construction, and a civic street presence anchored by the deep covered porch.

archetypes.title: Ev Charging Hub Mobility Station
archetypes.description: The EV Charging Hub & Mobility Station is a purpose-built urban infrastructure typology that combines fast-charging forecourts for electric vehicles with activated ground-floor amenities — cafés, waiting lounges, and micro-retail — to transform the utilitarian act of charging into a dwell-worthy public destination. Each hub integrates a prominent canopy or shade structure over the charging bays, supported by a compact service building of 1–2 storeys housing passenger amenities and energy management systems. The typology draws on sustainable design languages ranging from solar-integrated steel canopies to living green walls and mass-timber structures, signalling clean energy values through architectural expression. Sites are typically corner or mid-block urban infill plots with direct street frontage, generous forecourt paving, and landscape buffers that humanise the car-dominant programme. As EV adoption accelerates, these hubs function as the 21st-century successor to the petrol station, recast as civic-minded, pedestrian-friendly mobility nodes.

archetypes.title: Graduate Family Housing
archetypes.description: Graduate family housing provides subsidized residential accommodation for postgraduate students with dependents, typically developed and managed by universities on or adjacent to their campuses. These mid-rise buildings balance the density demands of urban university districts with the domestic scale and amenity requirements of family living — larger units, shared laundry, play areas, and community rooms. Architecturally they occupy a transitional character between institutional and residential, often clad in collegiate brick with contemporary detailing to signal both permanence and livability. Corner conditions and glazed stair towers are common compositional devices, and ground-floor activation through retail or community uses supports campus life. Sustainability features such as solar panels and balconies are increasingly standard in newer developments.

archetypes.title: High Tech Structural Arena
archetypes.description: The High Tech Structural Arena is a large-span civic sports and entertainment venue defined by expressive structural systems that are as visually legible as they are performative. These buildings celebrate engineering honesty — cable nets, exposed steel trusses, geodesic skins, and tensile canopies are worn as architectural identity rather than concealed. Programs typically include multi-purpose bowl seating, concourse retail, hospitality clubs, and flexible event floors suitable for concerts, sport, and exhibitions. The typology spans from mid-century tensile pioneers to contemporary parametric envelopes, always prioritising span, drama, and urban presence. Street-facing facades are animated by structural expression, large glazed concourses, and landmark rooflines visible from city approaches.

archetypes.title: Intermodal Transit Hub
archetypes.description: The intermodal transit hub is a large-footprint civic infrastructure building that consolidates rail, bus, metro, and active-transport modes under one roof, acting as a gateway node in the urban mobility network. Architecturally it is defined by its signature long-span roof structure — whether a sculptural steel exoskeleton, a monumental Beaux-Arts trainshed, a mass-timber arch hall, or a utilitarian steel-frame shed — that shelters vast concourse volumes and passenger circulation. The building typically presents a strong civic frontage to the street with generous glazed bays, covered drop-off canopies, and direct pedestrian connections to the public realm. Program includes ticketing halls, waiting concourses, retail and food-and-beverage, platform shelters, and back-of-house operations. Its scale and visibility make it a landmark within its district, with architectural ambition calibrated to the era and budget of the transit authority.

archetypes.title: Junction Converted Industrial Loft
archetypes.description: The Junction Converted Industrial Loft typology transforms early-twentieth-century factory and warehouse buildings into mixed-use live-work, creative-office, and retail destinations. Original heavy-timber or steel structural frames are preserved behind deep-red or buff brick envelopes punctuated by large multi-pane steel-framed windows that once lit factory floors. Adaptive reuse interventions range from sympathetic restoration of arched ground-floor openings and exposed wood trusses to contemporary rooftop glazed additions and green roofs. The buildings sit hard to the sidewalk in tight urban grain, activating street edges with generous ground-floor glazing and retained industrial character. Character details such as ghost signage, reclaimed brick, and expressed concrete banding distinguish this typology from new-build industrial pastiche.

archetypes.title: Large Art Museum Gallery
archetypes.description: Large art museum galleries are major civic anchor institutions housing permanent collections, touring exhibitions, and public programming across expansive floor plates. The typology spans an extraordinary range of architectural expression — from Beaux-Arts neoclassical palaces to parametric deconstructivist sculptures, from biophilic earth-sheltered pavilions to adaptive-reuse industrial conversions. Programmatically, they demand column-free gallery halls, controlled-light exhibition rooms, grand public atria, loading docks, conservation labs, and generous civic forecourts. Their civic presence commands prominent urban sites, waterfront locations, or cultural campuses, and their architecture is frequently treated as a statement of civic identity and cultural ambition. Scale is invariably large, with floor plates exceeding 2,000 sqm and heights ranging from low-profile earth-integrated pavilions to multi-storey monumental institutions.

archetypes.title: Mid Century Distribution Warehouse
archetypes.description: The mid-century distribution warehouse is a low-rise utilitarian building type developed primarily from the 1940s through 1970s to serve urban freight, wholesale, and light manufacturing networks. Characterised by deep floor plates, minimal fenestration, and a street-facing loading dock rhythm, these structures prioritise operational efficiency over architectural expression. Facades range from painted concrete masonry unit (CMU) blocks to corrugated metal cladding and board-formed concrete, reflecting the pragmatic material culture of postwar industrial construction. The typology sits directly on the street edge in dense urban industrial zones, with raised dock platforms and overhead doors defining the public face. Contemporary adaptations increasingly reinterpret the form with expressive structure — glulam arches, glazed gable ends — while retaining the single-storey large-span interior logic.

archetypes.title: Modern Big Box Logistics
archetypes.description: Modern big-box logistics facilities are large-footprint, single- or multi-storey warehouse and distribution buildings optimised for freight throughput, pallet storage, and last-mile or regional supply-chain operations. Their defining architectural features are repetitive dock-door bays along long operational facades, clear-span structural systems allowing column-free interiors, and a compact office or reception pod articulated in glazing at the building corner or entrance. The typology ranges from compact urban infill distribution centres with multi-level truck ramps to sprawling single-storey fulfilment sheds on suburban logistics parks, reflecting the full spectrum of e-commerce and industrial supply-chain demand. Facades are typically tilt-up concrete, insulated metal cladding, or composite panel systems with minimal ornamentation, expressing an honest industrial aesthetic tempered by branding, landscaping, and occasional biophilic gestures on contemporary examples.

archetypes.title: Outdoor Sports Stadium
archetypes.description: The outdoor sports stadium typology encompasses large-footprint spectator venues designed around an open playing field, with tiered seating bowls rising from street level to form a continuous or segmented ring. These structures serve as civic landmarks, anchoring neighborhoods with monumental scale and high pedestrian activity on event days. Architecturally, they range from expressive high-tech steel-and-ETFE shells to heritage brick arenas, biophilic mass-timber bowls, and utilitarian exposed-steel grandstands, each reflecting the era and ambition of their commissioning city. The exterior facade wraps the seating bowl and back-of-house concourses, functioning as a billboard-scale urban presence visible from surrounding streets and transit corridors. Program typically includes ticketing gates, concession concourses, press boxes, VIP suites, and at larger scales, integrated retail or hospitality at grade.

archetypes.title: Parisian Mid Rise
archetypes.description: The Parisian mid-rise is a quintessential European urban building type defined by Haussmann-era proportion, stone facades, and the seamless integration of ground-floor commerce with upper-floor residential or office use. Typically five to seven storeys, these perimeter-block buildings line boulevards with a continuous street wall punctuated by wrought-iron balconies, tall double-hung windows, and a mansard or zinc-clad attic storey. The typology spans from canonical Second Empire limestone blocks to Art Nouveau corner pieces, early-20th-century brick variants, and contemporary hybrid retrofits that graft glass penthouses onto historic stone plinths. Ground floors open generously to the pavement through arched arcade bays, shopfronts with canvas awnings, or glazed retail galleries, animating the street at all hours. The archetype anchors urban grain, enforces boulevard alignment, and projects civic elegance through material richness and tectonic restraint.

archetypes.title: Parkitecture
archetypes.description: Parkitecture refers to the rustic architectural style developed by the United States National Park Service in the early twentieth century, blending hand-hewn log construction, rough-cut stone masonry, and heavy timber framing into buildings that feel organically rooted in their natural surroundings. The typology encompasses visitor centers, ranger stations, lodges, and recreational facilities designed to harmonize with wilderness landscapes while providing durable public amenities. Characterized by generous covered porches, massive stone chimneys, steeply pitched shingle or shake roofs, and exposed structural timbers, these structures project an aesthetic of rugged craftsmanship and romantic naturalism. The style spans scales from a single-story frontier cabin to a multi-story lodge complex, unified by the consistent use of unfinished local materials and a warm, earthen palette. Parkitecture remains a beloved and widely reproduced vernacular for recreational facilities, park gatehouses, and nature-adjacent civic buildings.

archetypes.title: Postmodern Community Rec Centre
archetypes.description: The postmodern community recreation centre is a civic building typology that prioritises expressive architectural identity over functional anonymity, signalling public ownership through bold form, colour, and material play. Programs typically include gymnasiums, multi-purpose halls, fitness suites, aquatic facilities, and community meeting rooms arranged around a legible public entry sequence. The archetype spans a wide stylistic range — from exuberant primary-colour panelled volumes with porthole windows to contextual brick pavilions with patterned brickwork, to parametric deconstructivist metal-clad forms and sculptural concrete shells with geometric apertures. Common to all variants is a strong street presence, a clearly articulated main entrance, and a civic generosity of scale that distinguishes the building from its residential and commercial neighbours. The typology celebrates architecture as community identity-making, treating the building facade as a communicative surface.

Programmed with inpatient wards, emergency department, operating theatres, diagnostic imaging, outpatient clinics, and administrative offices. Architectural expression spans heritage pavilion-style pride, utilitarian mid-century district hospitals, contemporary teaching-hospital complexes, and new biophilic wellness-focused facilities — a building type with remarkable stylistic range driven by era, clinical philosophy, and site constraints.

archetypes.title: Research Laboratory
archetypes.description: Research laboratories encompass a broad spectrum of building typologies united by the demand for highly serviced, technically complex interiors supporting scientific investigation, experimentation, and discovery. Programs range from wet chemistry and biology labs to physics instrumentation suites, cleanrooms, and computational research facilities, often requiring deep floor plates, generous floor-to-floor heights, and robust mechanical infrastructure. Architecturally the typology ranges from expressive high-tech glass-and-steel structures that celebrate their mechanical systems to neoclassical collegiate institutions, biophilic mass-timber campuses, and utilitarian brutalist containment facilities. The building's character is frequently shaped by the tension between transparency and security, between openness to collaboration and the containment requirements of hazardous research. Across all variants, robust MEP infrastructure — exhaust stacks, fume hoods, chilled-water risers — is a defining architectural signature.

archetypes.title: Research Laboratory Innovation Hub
archetypes.description: The Research Laboratory Innovation Hub is an institutional building type that combines advanced scientific research facilities with collaborative innovation spaces, typically serving universities, biotech clusters, or public research agencies. These buildings balance highly serviced wet and dry lab floors with open co-working zones, seminar rooms, and maker spaces, promoting cross-disciplinary exchange. Architecturally, they range from stacked contemporary volumes with generous glazing to monolithic brutalist concrete frames with exposed structure, reflecting the intellectual rigor of their programs. The typology often incorporates rooftop greenhouses, solar canopies, or biophilic elements as signals of sustainability-focused research missions. Street-level activation through glazed lobbies and café frontages connects the institution to the urban fabric.

archetypes.title: Residential Superblock
archetypes.description: The residential superblock is a large-footprint, mid-rise apartment typology that occupies one or more full city blocks, providing high-density housing within a unified architectural composition. These buildings typically consolidate ground-floor retail or civic uses beneath stacked residential floors, with shared courtyard or roof amenities buffering the interior from the street. The typology spans a wide range of architectural movements — from parametric sculptural forms and Haussmann-era classical blocks to mass-timber biophilic complexes and brutalist megastructures — unified by their monumental urban scale and perimeter block logic. Facades are designed to address the street continuously, maintaining an active edge condition while upper floors step back, cantilever, or articulate to reduce visual bulk. As a cornerstone of urban residential density strategies, the superblock balances neighborhood-scale presence with internal community amenity.

archetypes.title: Science Engineering Lab Complex
archetypes.description: A science and engineering laboratory complex is a purpose-built academic research facility designed to house wet and dry labs, collaborative maker spaces, lecture halls, and faculty offices within a single integrated building. These complexes typically prioritize flexible open floor plates, robust MEP infrastructure for fume hoods and specialized equipment, and generous glazing to promote visibility into active research spaces. Architecturally they range from expressive parametric forms signaling institutional ambition to restrained brutalist blocks valued for structural pragmatism, to contemporary mass-timber hybrids reflecting sustainability mandates. The building type occupies a prominent position on university campuses or urban research districts, often serving as a gateway structure that communicates the institution's scientific identity to the public realm.

archetypes.title: Second Empire Civic Building
archetypes.description: The Second Empire Civic Building is a monumental institutional typology drawn from mid-to-late 19th-century French-influenced American civic architecture, characterized by its signature mansard roof, rusticated stone base, and hierarchical facade composition. These structures served as courthouses, city halls, post offices, fire stations, and municipal offices — embodying civic authority through classical ornamentation, projecting pavilions, and prominent corner or central clock towers. Facades are composed of dressed limestone or granite ashlar, articulated by cornices, pilasters, arched window surrounds, and sculptural relief panels. The mansard roofline — clad in slate or standing-seam metal with dormer windows — provides a distinctive silhouette that signals civic importance on the urban skyline. Buildings of this type anchor civic squares and major street corners, typically set back behind balustrades, grand entry stairs, and street-tree plantings.

archetypes.title: Student Residence Tower
archetypes.description: Student residence towers are purpose-built vertical housing typologies serving university and college populations, combining private sleeping units with shared amenity floors, study lounges, dining, and ground-level activation. These buildings typically occupy urban infill or campus-edge sites, rising between 8 and 14 storeys to maximize bed counts on constrained footprints. Architectural expression ranges from biophilic mass-timber and curtain-wall hybrids to raw board-formed concrete brutalist slabs, reflecting differing institutional philosophies around student life and sustainability. Ground floors are consistently activated with transparent glazing revealing common rooms, fitness centres, or retail, reinforcing pedestrian engagement along the street. The typology prioritizes communal identity, durable materiality, and a legible public presence befitting an institutional landmark.

archetypes.title: Student Union Campus Centre

These buildings are characterised by generous public interiors, expressive architectural gestures that signal welcome and identity, and a strong relationship to campus pedestrian networks. Programmatically they balance large-span social halls with intimate breakout spaces, often incorporating cafes, event venues, and student government offices. Architecturally they range from expressive mass-timber biophilic complexes to brutalist concrete landmarks, reflecting the era and institutional culture of their campus. Their frontages are typically highly transparent at ground level to draw students in from surrounding quads and streets.

archetypes.title: Ttc Streetcar Platform Stop
archetypes.description: The TTC Streetcar Platform Stop is a mid-block transit infrastructure typology representing Toronto's surface rapid transit network, providing sheltered boarding platforms embedded within street rights-of-way. These stops range from enclosed heritage-character shelters to open-air contemporary canopy structures, all designed to serve the Bombardier Flexity low-floor streetcar fleet operating on dedicated or shared track. Architecturally the typology spans over a century of transit design language, from red-brick and patinated-copper heritage pavilions to sleek glass-and-aluminum contemporary enclosures and biophilic green-roof canopies. Each variant prioritizes passenger weather protection, wayfinding signage, tactile platform edges, and clear sightlines to approaching vehicles. The stops function as small-scale civic anchors along commercial corridors, reinforcing the identity of Toronto's mixed-use street fabric.

archetypes.title: University Academic Complex
archetypes.description: The University Academic Complex archetype encompasses the full spectrum of higher-education building typologies, from landmark heritage halls to cutting-edge parametric research pavilions. These structures house lecture theatres, seminar rooms, faculty offices, libraries, and interdisciplinary laboratories within massing that ranges from compact urban infill blocks to sprawling classical colonnades. Architecturally the typology is defined by a strong institutional presence on the street, legible entry sequences, and facades that communicate civic purpose — whether through carved limestone ornament, biophilic mass-timber screens, or solar-integrated curtain wall. Sustainability credentials are increasingly embedded in the building fabric itself, with living walls, green roofs, and exposed structural systems becoming markers of progressive academic identity. The four variants represented here span neoclassical Georgian, contemporary high-tech, biophilic mass-timber, and brutalist-industrial research-lab expressions.

archetypes.title: University Library
archetypes.description: The university library is a major civic-institutional anchor on campus, providing collections, collaborative study, digital research, and community gathering under one roof. These buildings are defined by their architectural ambition — each generation of university library reflects the design values of its era, from Brutalist concrete fortresses to biophilic mass-timber pavilions. Facades range from sculptural corten arches and patterned glass curtainwalls to load-bearing stone roundhouses with ceremonial forecourts. Street presence is deliberate and monumental, with generous entrance stairs, transparent ground floors revealing reading rooms within, and carefully landscaped public approaches. The typology balances institutional gravitas with inviting permeability, signaling intellectual openness to the broader campus and city.

archetypes.title: Vertical Farm Indoor Agriculture
archetypes.description: Vertical farm indoor agriculture buildings integrate controlled-environment crop production into urban structures, stacking hydroponic or aeroponic growing layers across multiple floors to produce food within or adjacent to city populations. These buildings range from mid-rise glass curtain-wall towers with visible grow-lighting and robotic equipment to low-rise industrial retrofits topped with rooftop glasshouses, each expressing their agricultural program through transparency, grow-light glow, or greenhouse superstructures. Facades often reveal the interior farming operations — lush green plant rows, LED grow-light arrays, and automated racking systems — blurring the boundary between food production and urban spectacle. The typology can take the form of a sleek contemporary tower, a compact opaque controlled-environment block, a mass-timber high-rise, or an adaptive reuse of legacy industrial fabric. As urban food resilience becomes a planning priority, vertical farms are increasingly treated as civic infrastructure with public-facing ground-floor retail and educational programs.

archetypes.title: Vertiport Evtol Facility
archetypes.description: A vertiport and eVTOL facility is a next-generation air mobility transit hub designed to receive, charge, and dispatch electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft within or adjacent to the urban fabric. The typology blends terminal building functions — passenger check-in, waiting lounges, and ground-side connectivity — with rooftop or elevated landing pads engineered for rotorcraft clearance and noise attenuation. Architecturally, vertiports range from compact infill termini integrated into existing transit nodes to freestanding contemporary towers with dedicated rooftop flight decks. The building program typically includes ticketing and lounge space, eVTOL charging bays, operations control rooms, and intermodal connections to rail, bus, and ride-share. As a nascent typology, vertiports draw aesthetic cues from aviation, sustainability, and civic infrastructure — presenting a forward-looking image of urban air mobility.
